verdicts.question: Are the Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 in force (reported 1 April 2026)? Must kabadiwalas, scrap dealers, aggregators or 'entities involved in sorting' register on CPCB's portal (rule 9, rule 17 environmental compensation), and can individual shops register or only larger entities? What is the bulk-generator threshold (100 kg/day)?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits: no WebSearch was possible (session budget 200/200 already spent) and page fetches were refused, so nothing here is 'confirmed by snippet'. Cross-checked instead against other first-hand clusters in the repo. Corroborated there: S.O. 388(E) of 27 Jan 2026, in force 1 Apr 2026; definition (zb) 'informal waste collector' includes 'waste traders'; rule 9(1) sorters register with the local body; rule 17 EC on unregistered entities; rules 39(53)-(54) ward database and recognition; portal live for BWG registration since 31 May 2026; CPCB portal target 1 Oct 2026; BWG thresholds 100 kg/day, 20,000 sq m, 40,000 L/day (risk-guards, metrology-police, epr-portals, business brief). MISSED DEVELOPMENT: CPCB published 'Guidelines for levy of fees for the Centralised Online Portal under the SWM Rules, 2026' (cpcb.gov.in LatestFile/504_1790162155, file timestamp 23 Sep 2026; read first-hand for the business brief on 29 Sep 2026). Per that brief it sets one-time registration fees of Rs 1,000-5,000 for residential-society BWGs and Rs 2,000-10,000 for commercial BWGs plus 25% of that every year, and Rs 1,500-7,500 for sorting and processing sites (MRFs), and says BWGs file annual returns by 30 June. The answer's 'registration fee (if applicable) payable after activation of the payment gateway' and 'SPCB may charge a fee per CPCB guidelines' are therefore out of date, and a priced MRF/sorter band undercuts the flat statement that no non-BWG module exists. Not confirmed by any source I could reach: the Supreme Court 10 Aug 2026 order and its 29 Sep 2026 listing (yesterday's outcome is unknown and could change the EC picture), Gazette No. 360 of 28 Jan 2026, the swm.cpcb.gov.in module status, and BSWML's 6 Apr 2026 local thresholds (>100 flats, >5,000 sq m). Refined chain: the answer never places the founder's new roles. A pre-processor (PET flake/wash line, granulator, cable granulator, tyre shredder, e-waste dismantler, battery breaker, used-oil re-refiner) is a 'processing facility' needing local-body registration plus SPCB authorisation (rules 7, 41), and per the metrology cluster KSPCB consent (flakes/granules Orange; battery, e-waste, used oil under their own rules). Dry-waste centres/MRFs and yards that sort are rule-9 entities; compounders and manufacturers are outside SWM registration but must buy only from registered entities. Industrial by-products (bagasse, fly ash, slag, dross) are not municipal solid waste and fall outside this cluster (Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, KSPCB category codes), so the answer should say so.
verdicts.correction: Yes, in force: S.O. 388(E) notified 27 January 2026, effective 1 April 2026, replacing the 2016 rules (corroborated by four other clusters; PIB/gazette not re-opened this session). Who must register: every entity that sorts waste into recyclable and non-recyclable at an MRF registers with the local body (rule 9(1)), reports quarterly on the portal and deals only with registered entities; recyclers and processing facilities need local-body registration plus SPCB authorisation (rules 7, 41). In the founder's refined chain that means: dry-waste centres/MRFs and any yard that sorts or bales are rule-9 entities; every pre-processor (PET flake and wash lines, plastic and cable granulators, tyre shredders/pyrolysis, C&D crushers, e-waste dismantlers, battery breakers, used-oil re-refiners) is a processing facility needing SPCB authorisation and KSPCB consent (and, for e-waste, batteries, used oil and tyres, registration under those product rules instead); compounders and manufacturers have no SWM registration duty but must buy only from registered entities; industrial by-products (bagasse, fly ash, slag, dross, foundry sand) are not municipal solid waste and sit under the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules and KSPCB consent, not these rules. A kabadiwala shop that only buys and resells is an 'informal waste collector' (definition (zb) covers 'waste traders'); the rules put no registration duty on it but require the corporation to list informal collectors ward-wise on the portal (rule 39(53)) and to establish a system to recognise them (rule 39(54)). Rule 17 environmental compensation attaches to activities 'without registration as mandated', so the exposure is on unregistered sorting yards, MRFs and processors, not on a plain shop; the bigger risk for shops is exclusion, since bulk generators and RWAs may deal only with registered/authorised entities. NEW since the answer was written: CPCB's September 2026 'Guidelines for levy of fees for the Centralised Online Portal' (file dated 23 Sep 2026) set one-time registration fees of Rs 1,000-5,000 for residential-society bulk generators and Rs 2,000-10,000 for commercial ones, plus 25% of that annually, and Rs 1,500-7,500 for sorting and processing sites (MRFs); bulk generators file annual returns by 30 June. Budget the MRF band for every pilot yard and DWCC. Whether the MRF/sorter self-registration module is live yet is an open item (the answer said only the BWG module was live on 29 Sep 2026; rule 16(1) gave CPCB until about 1 Oct 2026). The Supreme Court's 10 Aug 2026 direction to frame EC guidelines was listed for 29 Sep 2026; the outcome is unknown and must be checked before telling any yard what a fine looks like. Bulk-generator threshold: any one of 100 kg/day of waste, 20,000 sq m floor area, or 40,000 L/day of water, covering residential societies, offices, institutions, hotels, malls and markets (corroborated by the business brief's read of the CPCB fee guideline). BSWML's local addition (>100 flats or >5,000 sq m site, circular of 6 Apr 2026) could not be verified this session; keep it as a configurable city flag. Decision unchanged except: add the fee bands to the yard/MRF onboarding checklist, add pre-processor and compounder as verification roles with their own permit fields, and keep industrial by-product listings out of SWM compliance logic. Ask: CPCB portal helpdesk (module status, fee guideline text), the pilot corporation's SWM wing (rule-9 registration path), counsel (29 Sep 2026 Supreme Court outcome).

verdicts.question: Under the SWM Rules 2026, who issues EBWGR (bulk waste generator) certificates and at what price? Can a network of kabadiwalas and yards supply compliant collection to Bengaluru apartment societies?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits as above: no snippet could be obtained. Corroborated by other repo clusters: only the local body issues EBWGR certificates, based on kg delivered to registered recyclers (public-systems brief); BSWML lost primary collection on 16 Aug 2025 and kept processing/disposal (dwcc-partners cluster, same Deccan Herald source); rule 9(7) MRF as drop-off/EPR uptake point. NOT corroborated anywhere and not confirmed by snippet: the Rs 12/kg cap by State notification of 4 March 2025, the Rs 8/kg market quote attributed to the Bengaluru Development Minister on 22 July 2026, the five named Authorised Waste Processors and their corporation mapping, the 90% vendor delisting (Aug 2025), the 5,837 surveyed bulk generators (5 May 2026), the BSWML MD's January 2026 admission, the three-year certificate validity (rule 10(6)) and the 'fee' wording of rule 39(38). These carry the decision ('use Rs 12/kg ceiling, Rs 8/kg market'), so they must be treated as unverified until someone opens the Deccan Herald (21 Dec 2025) and Hans India (22 Jul 2026) pages. MISSED DEVELOPMENT: CPCB's September 2026 portal fee guideline (file dated 23 Sep 2026) exists and, per the business brief that read it, describes BWGs registering, filing annual returns by 30 June and buying EBWGR certificates, with registration fee bands; the answer's 'no CPCB pricing norm is public' should be re-checked against that document (it may still be silent on the per-kg certificate price, which stays with each ULB's by-laws). Arithmetic: 'Rs 12/kg x 365 x kg/day' is consistent; the rule 5(2) one-year deadline computes to 27 Jan 2027 if counted from notification, but 1 Apr 2027 if counted from commencement, and the answer does not say which reading the rule text supports. Refined chain: EBWGR kilograms are earned at the hand-off where a registered processor or recycler receives the lot, i.e. when a yard's S3 bale or an MRF's S2 sorted lot moves to a registered pre-processor/recycler (S3 to S4), not at S1 collection; the answer should say the receiving party in the evidence pack must be a registered processing facility, which in the founder's model is the pre-processor, not the yard, so the pilot evidence chain runs household to kabadiwala to yard to registered pre-processor.
verdicts.correction: Issuer: only the local body (in Bengaluru, the city corporation for that area, working with BSWML) can generate an Extended Bulk Waste Generator Responsibility certificate on CPCB's portal; it equals the kilograms the corporation or its registered third party collected and delivered to registered processors or recyclers (rule 10), so Luma.Green reports into a certificate and never issues one. Price: the rules fix no national price; the cost is settled per CPCB guidance and each ULB's by-laws (Bengaluru's are due 31 March 2027). CPCB's September 2026 portal fee guideline (file dated 23 Sep 2026) is now public and covers BWG registration fees (Rs 1,000-5,000 residential, Rs 2,000-10,000 commercial, plus 25% a year) and says BWGs buy EBWGR certificates; whether it prices the certificate per kg is an open item to read off that PDF. Bengaluru's working numbers in the original answer (Rs 12/kg State cap by notification of 4 March 2025; about Rs 8/kg quoted by vendors per the Minister on 22 July 2026; BSWML's April 2026 property-tax formula of Rs 12/kg x 365 x kg/day) could not be verified this session and no other cluster confirms them; keep them as placeholders labelled 'unverified' in any model until the BSWML PDF and the 4 March 2025 notification are opened. Compliance for a kabadiwala network: bulk generators must hand dry, sanitary and special-care waste to the local body or an agency it authorises and may not engage unregistered entities (rule 6); RWAs above 5,000 sq m must use authorised waste pickers or recyclers within one year of notification (27 Jan 2027 if counted from notification, 1 Apr 2027 if from commencement; confirm the rule text); households hand over to authorised collectors as the local body directs (rule 5). So a kabadiwala network is compliant only once the corporation or BSWML authorises it or it works under an existing Authorised Waste Processor. The AWP roster, the August 2025 delisting and the 5,837-BWG survey are unverified this session; confirm directly with BSWML's bulk-waste cell. Refined chain: the EBWGR kilograms are earned when a registered processing facility receives the lot, so the pilot evidence pack must record the registered pre-processor or recycler that takes the yard's S3 bale (or an MRF's S2 sorted lot), with the yard's own rule-9 registration number; a kg-per-building report that stops at the yard will not support a certificate. Decision: unchanged in shape (serve sub-threshold buildings first, offer bulk generators a dry-waste kg report, open a dry-waste-only AWP conversation with BSWML), but mark the Rs 12/Rs 8 figures unverified and add 'registered pre-processor receipt' as a required field. Ask: BSWML bulk-waste cell (cap notification, AWP list, empanelment criteria), CPCB helpdesk (whether the Sep 2026 guideline prices EBWGR), counsel (rule 5(2) start date).

verdicts.question: Will the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) or BSWML recognise verified kabadiwalas as 'authorised' informal waste collectors, and what will Bengaluru's new SWM by-laws (due 31 March 2027) say? Do the 2026 rules add a separate household 'special care' stream (batteries, bulbs) and what bin colours do they prescribe?
verdicts.problems: Verification limits as above: no snippet could be obtained. Corroborated by other repo clusters: rules 39(53)-(54) ward database and recognition duty (risk-guards); by-laws due 31 Mar 2027 and corporation elections by 31 Dec 2026 (public-systems); five city corporations and 369 wards under the GBA, BSWML stripped of collection on 16 Aug 2025 with a DWCC or MRF per ward 'by partnering with ragpickers' (dwcc-partners); Hasiru Dala's 11,300+ occupational ID cards (dwcc-partners); four-stream segregation with special care as a mandatory stream (design-facts). CONTRADICTION on bin colours: the answer says 'the gazette contains no colour code' and that only a reporting form mentions green, blue and black bins. The design-facts cluster, which read the gazette PDF (OpenCity copy) first-hand on 30 Sep 2026, quotes the rules directing local bodies that bins 'for storage of wet waste shall be painted green, those for storage of dry waste shall be printed blue and if required in public toilets bins painted in red may be placed for sanitary waste', with no colour for special care and the annual-return forms counting green, blue and black bins. So the rules do prescribe colours for public and storage bins (green wet, blue dry, red sanitary), leaving household bins and special care uncoded; the answer's flat 'no colour code' is wrong and the CWAS deck's black-for-special-care is a convention, not a rule. Not confirmed by any source I could reach: the UDD order of 2 Sep 2025, building by-laws effective 14 May 2026, the BAF quote of 2 May 2026, the BSWML workshop of 18 Apr 2026 (700 people), the BBMP SWM Bye-laws 2020 notification date of 4 June 2020, rule 39(48) one deposition centre per 5 sq km, and the exact rule 3(1)(zx) item list. Refined chain: special-care waste (paint drums, pesticide containers, CFLs, tube lights, expired medicines, thermometers, batteries, sharps) and the residual-waste lots that every processing record must produce are exactly what the founder's 'authorised waste handler / co-processor / TSDF' role receives; the answer should map the special-care stream and residual lots to that role and to the KSPCB-authorised handler, and state that batteries and e-waste collected under the special-care stream can only be transferred to entities registered under the Battery and E-Waste Rules (the founder's battery breakers and e-waste dismantlers), never processed by a yard.
verdicts.correction: Recognition: nothing public commits GBA or BSWML to recognising kabadiwalas, but the rules make it a duty of each local body: a ward-wise portal database of everyone in collection, sorting, transport and recycling including informal waste pickers and traders (rule 39(53)) and a system to recognise and integrate them (rule 39(54)), with new SWM by-laws due by 31 March 2027 (rule 39(5)). In Bengaluru the local body is now each of the five city corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority (369 wards), with BSWML confined to processing and disposal since August 2025 while still running the bulk-generator programme; the state ordered a DWCC or MRF in every ward in partnership with waste pickers. No draft SWM by-law is known (this could not be re-checked this session), so the BBMP SWM Bye-laws 2020 and the Hasiru Dala ID-card precedent (11,300+ cards) remain the reference. Expect by-laws to carry forward waste-picker registration and DWCCs and to add four streams, special-care deposition points, the EBWGR price and fines; an 'authorised kabadiwala shop' category is undetermined and worth asking for in the objection window. Special care: yes, a separate mandatory household stream (wet, dry, sanitary, special care), covering items such as paint drums, pesticide containers, CFLs and tube lights, expired medicines, mercury thermometers, waste batteries and sharps; local bodies run deposition centres and registered MRFs may serve as deposition points, while e-waste and batteries stay under their own rules (item list and the per-5-sq-km spacing not re-verified this session). In the founder's refined chain, special-care items and every processing record's residual-waste lot route to the 'authorised waste handler / co-processor / TSDF' role, and batteries and e-waste collected through the stream may only be transferred to entities registered under the Battery and E-Waste Rules (the founder's battery breakers and e-waste dismantlers), never opened at a yard. Bin colours, corrected: the rules do contain a colour direction for local-body bins, quoted first-hand by the design-facts cluster: bins 'for storage of wet waste shall be painted green, those for storage of dry waste shall be printed blue and if required in public toilets bins painted in red may be placed for sanitary waste'; special-care waste has no prescribed colour, and the annual-return forms still count green, blue and black bins (black being the old domestic-hazardous colour). Household bins are not colour-coded by the rules. So show green = wet, blue = dry, red = sanitary as rule-backed defaults, treat black (CWAS convention) or orange for special care as a city-configurable choice until Bengaluru's by-laws fix it, and never use green on a material chip because households read it as wet waste. Decision otherwise unchanged. Ask: Special Commissioner (SWM) of the pilot corporation and GBA on by-law timetable; BSWML on deposition centres; Hasiru Dala on the ID-card and trader treatment under the 2020 by-laws.
